newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX electricity up on San Onofre 2 nuke outage.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX electricity up on San Onofre 2 nuke outage.

text.p: NYMEX electricity futures were trading higher Monday, taking support from an unexpected outage at the San Onofre 2 nuclear power unit in California, market sources said.
Southern California Edison Co said it expects the 1,070 megawatt (MW) San Onofre 2 nuclear unit in San Clemente, Calif., to remain off line until July 15 following a shutdown Sunday.
The unit was shut to replace its charge line check valves after scaling output to back to 90 percent of capacity last Thursday.
The adjoining San Onofre 3 nuclear unit, rated at 1,080 MW, remained in cold shutdown after being taken off line April 12 for refueling and was scheduled to resume operations around July 10.

The outage boosted power futures and short term physical prices Monday morning, with values receiving more strength on SoCal Edison's announcement the unit would be out of service until the middle of the month.
"Initially people thought the outage was going to last only several days," said one Houston-based futures trader.

As of 1215 EDT, August Palo Verde (PV) futures were trading up $1.89 at $34.15 per megawatt hour (MWh) following exchanges at $33.30-35.10 per MWh, while September was up 79 cents at $28.50 after trades at $28.25-29.00 per MWh.
August California Oregon Border (COB) was trading up $1.23 at the day's high of $23.60 after trade as low as $22.85, while September was bid at $22.80 from Friday's settlement at $22.35 per MWh.
NYMEX said that as of 1140 EDT an estimated 10 COB and 143 PV contracts had traded.
Also as of 1215 EDT, August Henry Hub natural gas futures were trading up 0.6 cents at $2.145 per million British thermal units.
The latest six to 10 day forecasts showed temperatures in the Pacific Northwest would average below normal, while those in the Southwest would run above normal.

The WNP-2 nuclear plant in Washington state continued to await clearance from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission before beginning start-up operations, a spokesman for the plant said Thursday, adding the unit would be "physically ready" to resume operations by late tonight or early Friday.

Several Western coal-fired power units were set to return to the power grid by this week, including a 670 MW unit at Centralia, Wash., a 330 MW Colstrip unit in Montana and a 260 MW Hayden unit in Colorado.
Late Friday, the Western Systems Coordinating Council board approved a derating of the Pacific Intertie transmission sytem to 6,300 MW from the current 7,200 MW, which was effective Saturday.
